heading: Furari
text:
The concept of cute animals on t-shirts was done countless times before, especially in Indonesia. The approach to this trend normally falls on either the forestry/jungle side or the domesticated cute side. I knew in order to appeal to audiences, we needed a fresh plan - something that struck the in-between but also added another element.

There were now two challenges for me: to incorporate all themes into one mascot, and to figure out how it all makes sense in one brand. I pushed out the sweetest, most pleasing visuals while referencing organic curves in my artwork, always keeping in mind the platforms this would be marketed on.

heading: Appetizing Apparel
text:
The target demographic for these products are normally fond of current trends. My client and I hopped on many discussions to plan out the strategy for creating the mascots.

Believe it or not, the direction of this project was very different at the start; aiming for a petite and rounded approach. The outcome was something pure - but oddly, not quite fitting for the target audience.

heading: Adopting Trends
text:
We explored the quirky nature of the regular house cat - unbothered, domesticated, but always up to something.

We took those ideas and came up with the two we found strongest, then pushed them through apparel, packaging and signage until the character held up everywhere it appeared.

heading: Bangun Citra Irawan
text:
Bangun Citra Irawan is a company run by the greatest man I know, my dad. So when he rattled me for a logo and a brand system, I delivered one to him without hesitation.

BCI aims to be beyond the norm, to stand out above all else. The company wanted to not feel rigid, so we looked to something that exudes future-facing. BCI was never about one product, but many variations of services.

The rounded approach was favoured, with the yellow dot representing the morning sun. The brand system features a strong blue, paired with a dark and light shade for official purposes. Additionally, the batik pattern uses assets present in the logo to extend the branding while staying true to our Indonesian roots.

heading: The Heir of Time
text:
The Heir of Time was a progressive request for my design work. They are run by Just Just Productions, an upcoming animated TV series set in a sci-fi/fantasy world. It was an ambitious project that required some design nudging to progress.

I was brought on initially to design a title graphic for the show's intro, but quickly offered to upgrade my services to brand the entire project.

heading: Out of Orbit
text:
The Heir of Time follows an elven princess caught between an intergalactic war, where she also struggles to control her time-jumping abilities. Marco from Just Just Productions asked me to design a logo and title graphic that suited this mix of ideas - a fantasy feel that belongs to a sci-fi IP. The title graphic shown to me was cheap and generic, and said nothing about the scope of the series.

For this series to grow into an IP, they needed a brand. The project was split across different media and never really captured the same energy for each piece of content. They were excellent at drawing first impressions, but struggled to maintain or reinvite viewers. They needed a colour palette, a typeface, and a glow up. Every great franchise has consistency in branding - Star Wars, Dune, Arcane.

heading: The Royal Flush
text:
After several iterations and two discussion calls, the logo became a mix of splitting lines and sharp edges.

The splitting lines symbolise the diverging timelines, and how the main character, Sel, jumps back and forth uncontrollably throughout the story. Thin, elongated rectangles as the building blocks of the letters, combined with curves and a scratched gold texture, marry the sci-fi and fantasy themes together.

Branding started where the logomark ended: the colours. We settled on purple to separate the main brand from the factions while complementing the gold accents. Marco and his team were ecstatic with the direction and took it straight to their MCM Comic Con stand.

heading: Trinity in the Stars
text:
The identity of Xalgoria was far more open than the other two factions, and I was granted creative freedom. I worked with complementary orange and purple while sprinkling in neon green to maximise the dystopian feel. A fun spin on the Xalgorian lingo was taking Japanese and Chinese letterforms and smoothing them in Illustrator to create alien typography.

For the other two I kept a straightforward approach. For the FIS, rigid and pointed edges illustrate their cold nature, and mundane icons repeated over and over create a familiar human look.

The Armelion relied heavily on curves, inspired by vines and flowers. The icons were simplified into basic shapes to contrast with the defined line detail behind them.

heading: Pastel Mumu
text:
Pastel Mumu was a spontaneous request from a family friend. They sell Indonesian pastries in the heart of Australia. They did not need anything fancy or exclusive - just a logo that playfully depicts what is on offer in store.

I needed to create something ultimately versatile, primarily for stickers. Despite the initial deal being a logo and a colour palette, I developed the concept further into a full brand, to see it flourish into a proper chain in Sydney.

heading: New Cities, Old Recipes
text:
The initial logo presented to me was very outdated. It lacked the basic logo design concepts that would have made it strong, unique and versatile - too many words, too many colours, and no hierarchy. Despite that, the brief and the early iterations made it clear the product needed to be represented in the logomark.

Pastel Mumu wanted to expand beyond a single shop, across Sydney, not only for deliveries but for new stores. Sydney is a bright and colourful place - believe me, I have been there. Blending in with the city mattered for the brand, while still showing the hospitality Indonesian culture always brings to guests.

heading: Crispy Creations
text:
Growing up, I have devoured countless pastels - I knew this pastry inside out. The sketching progressed quicker than usual, and I iterated several designs that pivoted to the word Mumu integrated into the crust. The final result felt natural and justified.

The mandarin orange and sandy yellow were an excellent pairing, with cream to wrap it all together. To push the brand beyond a static palette, hot pink screamed to audiences perfectly and became the final ingredient.

A pastel is not one fixed recipe - they come with different toppings, and the randomness pleases with each bite. To capture that, I turned to pattern: squiggles, swirls and dots standing in for the toppings, combined into one versatile brand pattern.
